passages.t: Abijam, and a lamp for David's sake
passages.happening:
‘In the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king of Judah’ (verse 1), and he reigns three years in Jerusalem. His mother is Maacah daughter of Abishalom (verse 2). He walks in all his father's sins, ‘and his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been’ (verse 3).

“Nevertheless, for the sake of David, the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong” (verse 4). For David had done what was right all his days, ‘except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite’ (verse 5). There is war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all Abijam's days, and when he dies, his son Asa reigns in his place (verses 6-8).
passages.hearers:
The story now settles into the rhythm that carries the rest of Kings: reign after reign, back and forth between Judah and Israel, each king dated by the other kingdom's king and judged by one standard. Judah's kings are measured against David, and Israel's against Jeroboam.

Abijam reigned about 913 to 911 BC. Chronicles calls him Abijah. He deserved to lose the throne, and he did not, because of the promise to David. The lamp is a picture of a family line kept alive, and the promise holds the line steady even through a bad king.

The note about David is honest. The book that measures every king against David remembers his great sin in the same breath. David's faithfulness was not sinlessness; it was a heart that never turned to other gods.

Dates like these are approximate. The kings' reigns overlap, and kingdoms counted a king's first year in different ways, which scholars such as Edwin Thiele have tried to work out.
passages.later: Matthew's family tree of Jesus runs through these kings: ‘Solomon the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asa’ (Matthew 1:7).
passages.asks: Abijam kept a throne he did not deserve, for someone else's sake. Ask what you have received because of another person's faithfulness. And ask what faithfulness of yours might keep a lamp burning for those who come after you.

passages.t: Asa: a devoted heart, and a bargain with Aram
passages.happening:
Asa becomes king of Judah in Jeroboam's twentieth year and reigns forty-one years (verses 9-10). “And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done” (verse 11). He drives the male shrine prostitutes out of the land and removes the idols his fathers had made. He even removes his grandmother Maacah from her place as queen mother, because she had made a detestable Asherah pole, and he cuts it down and burns it in the Kidron Valley (verses 12-13). ‘The high places were not removed, but Asa’s heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days’ (verse 14).

But there is war with Baasha king of Israel, who fortifies Ramah to cut off Judah (verses 16-17). Asa takes all the silver and gold left in the treasuries of the temple and the palace and sends them to Ben-hadad king of Aram in Damascus, asking him to break his treaty with Baasha (verses 18-19). Ben-hadad attacks Israel's northern towns, and Baasha withdraws (verses 20-21). Asa's men carry off the stones and timber of Ramah and build up Geba and Mizpah (verse 22). In his old age Asa's feet become diseased, and when he dies, his son Jehoshaphat reigns (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
Asa reigned about 911 to 870 BC, the first reform since the kingdom divided. The queen mother held an official position at the court of Judah, and her name is recorded for nearly every king; removing Maacah was a public act, not only a family quarrel. The Hebrew of verses 2 and 10 calls her the mother of both Abijam and Asa. The BSB, like many translations, takes her as Asa's grandmother, since mother can mean ancestress in Hebrew, and she evidently kept her rank into a second reign. The Kidron Valley, east of the city, became the usual place to destroy such objects.

The high places, local hilltop shrines, were often left standing even by kings who were praised. Kings notes it each time, until Hezekiah and Josiah remove them.

Ramah lay about five miles north of Jerusalem on the main road, so fortifying it choked Judah's way north. Asa's answer was to pay Ben-hadad, grandson of Hezion, to turn on Israel. Treaties between kings were often described as passing from father to son. The Hebrew word for Asa's gift often means a bribe. Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah and Chinnereth, near the Sea of Galilee, were on Israel's northern frontier.

The same word for a whole heart is used for Abijam, whose heart was not fully devoted (verse 3), and for Asa, whose heart was (verse 14).
passages.later: Chronicles tells of a prophet who rebuked Asa for the bargain: “Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand” (2 Chronicles 16:7). A psalm puts the choice simply: ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.hard:
Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD, yet he paid a pagan king to attack Israel. Does the text approve?

Kings reports the alliance without an open verdict, and it worked: Baasha withdrew. But the narrator's details lean critical. Asa emptied the treasury he had just filled (verse 15), paid what the Hebrew calls a bribe, and invited a foreign power to attack fellow Israelites, opening a door Aram would use against both kingdoms for generations. The parallel account in Chronicles is open about it: the prophet Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on the king of Aram instead of the LORD.

Readers differ on how to weigh this against the praise of verse 14. Most conclude that the verdict on Asa's heart describes his lifelong loyalty to the LORD against idols, while this episode shows that a loyal king could still fail to trust God in a crisis.
passages.asks: Asa tore down idols and then, under pressure, emptied God's house to buy a foreign king's help. Ask what you reach for first when you are hemmed in. And ask whether there is an area where your loyalty to God is real but your trust in him is thin.

passages.t: Nadab, Baasha, and the end of Jeroboam's house
passages.happening:
‘In the second year of Asa’s reign over Judah, Nadab son of Jeroboam became king of Israel, and he reigned two years’ (verse 25). He does evil and walks in his father's sin (verse 26). Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, plots against him and kills him at Gibbethon, a Philistine town that Israel was besieging, and reigns in his place (verses 27-28).

As soon as he is king, Baasha strikes down Jeroboam's whole household, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servant Ahijah the Shilonite’ (verse 29), because of the sins Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit (verse 30). Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah, ‘And Baasha did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Nadab's short reign fell about 910 to 909 BC, and Baasha's about 909 to 886. Ahijah's word against Jeroboam's house (14:10) is fulfilled within two years of Jeroboam's death, and the first of the northern kingdom's many coups begins a pattern of violent turnover that marks its whole history. Israel had nine dynasties in about two hundred years, and eight of its kings lost the throne to a coup.

Gibbethon was a Philistine town on Israel's western edge, fought over for decades. Baasha kills his king in the middle of a siege.

The text records the killing of Jeroboam's household as the fulfillment of a prophet's word, and the next chapter will hold Baasha to account for it. God's word comes true through a violent man's ambition, and the violence is not made good by it. The household's death is told in a sentence and not dwelt on.
passages.later: Hosea later says the same of another bloody founder of a northern dynasty, Jehu: ‘soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu’ (Hosea 1:4).
passages.asks: Baasha destroyed Jeroboam's house for its sin and then walked in the same sin. Ask whether you condemn in others what you go on doing yourself. And ask what it would take to break a pattern rather than simply replace the people in it.
